checks: Each positive length contribution is a clipped affine function of t with slope magnitude at most one before normalizing. Taking infima preserves both monotonicities and the common N/M Lipschitz bound. Zero-volume fibers are harmless.

For arbitrary slopes a,b the two caps cover every positive interval on the base side (a−b)·(z−z₀)≥0. That whole side pays at least β by the normalized marginal depth. If a=b it is all bases. Since the inequality holds for every independent pair of slopes, attainment is unnecessary.

The convex hull of the positive interval lifts is a polytope in its relative base affine hull times the continuous line. At the lower endpoint a downward feasible motion would exist unless an active inequality had negative continuous coefficient. The analogous upward motion at the upper endpoint gives the other sign. Extending the two affine base graphs gives zero measured traces and preserves lower-dimensional base support.

Continuity and L(u)+R(u)≥β give a nonatomic probability supported on the actual closed target interval. For right closed rays 1−F(t) is valid including equality, and L+R≥β bounds that right tail. Vertical caps either carry the full target or none, and in the full case marginal depth supplies β. The corresponding median bound follows.
The original unnumbered CDF and endpoint-support passage gives the same probability and hypotheses. Its separate global-depth corollary is outside this candidate.

overlap.comparison: The earlier line-envelope theorem assumes absolute continuity in the whole ambient space and k≤1/2. Original mixed length over finite bases is singular when the base rank is positive, and β can exceed 1/2. The clipped fiber continuity and supporting graphs establish the different hypothesis regime.

The earlier coupling theorem takes one integer coordinate at a median and gives fixed domination factor 2 for its coupling outputs. The new law is an explicit CDF at any positive fiber of known marginal depth, in any base rank, with factor 1/β.
Its interval cap-circuit consequence controls a mark's depth in the prescribed interval. It does not construct a full nonatomic target law with all-cap domination.
